claims.text: An agricultural system has the same three parts as any system: inputs are what goes into the farm (physical inputs such as sun, rain and soil; human inputs of labour, skill and money; and bought inputs such as seed, fertiliser, fuel and tools), processes are what the farmer does on the farm (ploughing, sowing, tending, harvesting, feeding, milking, irrigating), and outputs are what comes out: products for the family or the market, and waste such as straw, dung and run-off.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Farms are classified along four independent pairs: subsistence farming feeds the farmer's family with little or nothing sold, commercial farming sells its produce for profit; arable farming grows crops, pastoral farming keeps animals; intensive farming uses high inputs per hectare for high yields, extensive farming uses low inputs per hectare over a large area; and a system may be any combination - a subsistence arable plot is intensive, a Karakul sheep run is extensive pastoral.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: The farming terms sort into four pairs, and the test is which pair each term belongs to: subsistence or commercial (who the food is for), arable or pastoral (crops or animals), intensive or extensive (inputs per hectare). Because the pairs are independent, a farm may be commercial and pastoral at once; inputs are what goes into the farm, outputs are what comes out of it, and the two words are not interchangeable.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: A maize garden in the north of Namibia shows the system in the round: inputs of rain in the wet months, household labour, seed kept from last year's harvest, a hand hoe and cattle manure; processes of clearing, hoeing the soil, sowing at the first rains, weeding and scaring birds from the ripening cobs; outputs of maize cobs eaten fresh, meal ground for the family, cattle fodder and garden waste to the compost.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Food shortages have natural causes (drought, floods, tropical storms, and pests or diseases such as locust swarms and army worm, which destroy standing crops) and human causes (war and displacement, which keep fields un-planted; poor transport, which strands food where it grows; and low investment in irrigation, storage and farming skills, which leaves yields small and losses high).

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: The effects of a food shortage follow a chain: harvests fail or food cannot reach people, so food prices rise; families then eat less, so undernutrition rises; children stop growing well, disease strikes weakened bodies more easily, so illness and death rates rise; and families may sell livestock or leave their land to find food, which deepens the loss of assets and income.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Sorting shortage causes correctly means asking two questions: natural or human, and cause or effect. Drought is a natural cause; war is a human cause; rising prices and undernutrition are effects that follow the shortage, not causes of it. The test is natural or human, and cause or effect.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Solutions to food shortages work on both sides of the balance: increasing supply - irrigation to cut dependence on rain, better seed and fertiliser to raise yields, control of pests, and roads and storage to cut losses - and reducing demand or diversifying food sources - food aid and grain reserves to bridge shortages, population programmes where growth outstrips land, and new trades so families can buy food grown elsewhere.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: A solution should be judged against the problem it fits: irrigation raises yields but costs money that small farmers may not have; food aid bridges a crisis but can undercut local growers if it arrives as cheap grain; so the judgement depends on the local situation - scale, cost and reliability.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: The Hardap Irrigation Scheme on the Fish River south of Mariental, southern Namibia, is a large commercial agricultural system: a dam completed in 1963 holds the river's summer floods, and about 1 100 hectares of irrigated land below it (approximate figure) grow lucerne (alfalfa), maize, wheat, vegetables and grapes, largely for fodder and produce markets, with heavy machinery, pumps, fertiliser and full-time labour among its inputs.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Hardap is a commercial, mixed, intensive farming system: commercial because its fodder, grain, vegetables and grapes are sold for profit; intensive because it combines high inputs per hectare - irrigation water pumped from the dam, fertiliser, machinery and a resident workforce - with high yields that dry-land farming in this low-rainfall area (under about 200 millimetres a year) could not produce; arable in its crops and pastoral in the livestock its fodder supports.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: The Sahel region of West Africa - the dry belt south of the Sahara, in countries such as Niger, Mali, Burkina Faso and Chad - suffers recurring food shortages: rainfall is low and unreliable, and in drought years such as 1984 and 2010-2012, harvests failed and millions needed food aid (over 18 million people across the region were at risk in 2012, approximate figure).

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: The Sahel's food shortages have linked causes: a natural cause - low, unreliable rain, in places under about 400 millimetres a year, failing further in drought years; and human causes - rapid population growth straining thin soils and firewood, overgrazing and tree clearance degrading the land, and conflict and displacement, as in Mali in 2012, keeping farmers from their fields.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: The Sahel shows both the effects of shortage and the solutions tried: effects include failed harvests and rising grain prices, undernutrition measured in the tens of millions of people, herders moving south with cattle as pastures fail, and families selling assets to buy food; solutions tried include grain banks and reserves run by cooperatives, tree-planting and terracing to hold soil and water, improved seed and small-scale irrigation, and food aid in the worst years.
